You scan the room through a haze of lamplight and cigar smoke. The Lamplight's main hall is built into the curve of a true rib, its mahogany bar following the bone's sweep like a horsehair seam. To your left, three merchants from the Merchant's Lung haggling too loudly over a game of knucklebones, their silk vests dark with damp from the canals. In the far booth, a Veil-marked woman in a plague-doctor's mask sits alone with a glass she hasn't touched, watching the door. Vess shifts beside you, the velvet of her sleeve brushing your arm. She doesn't follow your gaze. She already knows who's here.

Two of the Velvet Row girls are working the floor: Mira behind the bar pouring something amber, and Dallah upstairs — you can hear her laugh drifting through the floorboards, high and false. Old Harro is in his usual corner, mending a shoe by gaslight, though you suspect he's listening more than stitching. And near the street door, a new face: a broad man in a coat too heavy for the season, fingers drumming the table, eyes fixed on the back staircase. He hasn't ordered anything.

The blade bites deep, and the collector's eyes go wide with the particular surprise of a man who had not thought it would end this night. Blood spills hot across your hands, then runs cold and thin into the gutters where it swirls with the rainwater. He crumples against the slick cobbles, one hand still clutching the satchel of coins he'd been about to take from a widow two streets over. His mouth works soundlessly. Then it stops.

You stand over him, breathing hard, the rain washing the red from your knuckles in pale threads. Somewhere above, between the curving white arches of the god's old ribs, a crow takes flight with a ragged cry. Down here in the close dark of the alley, the only witnesses are the rats already creeping from the drainage grate, and the thin woman huddled in a doorway who has pressed both hands over her mouth. Her eyes are fixed on you—not with horror, but with a kind of desperate, feral gratitude. The collector's men will notice he hasn't returned by morning. They always do.

You drag the beggar into the shadow of a crooked rib and do what you do. He whimpers, he lies, he weeps — and then, when the rain has washed the last of his secrets out, he tells you a name that may or may not be true: *Velk the Quiet*, whispered in alleys near the salt docks. When you let him go, he scrambels into the gutter with one hand pressed to his ruined face, and the other denizens of the slum pull their hoods tighter, sliding their eyes from you as though you have become something the dead god's bones should not have to shelter. Somewhere a child begins to cry, and a woman spits at your feet and hurries away before you can turn. You feel the name settle in your mouth like a copper coin — useful, perhaps, but paid for in something you cannot spend back.

I'm not going to narrate that. Threatening to harm a child isn't something I'll roleplay, regardless of the setting or framing.

If you want to continue the adventure, I'm happy to narrate other actions — exploring the rain-soaked slum, investigating the dead god's ribs, encountering NPCs, or pursuing the scene in a different direction that doesn't involve violence against a child. What would you like to do instead?

The question hangs in the air between you like a coin balanced on its edge. Vess Corran does not look at you when she answers; she looks at the row of phlegm-yellow gas mantles along the back bar, watching them shudder in some draught you can't feel.

"Twenty," she says. "Up front. And twenty more for the room, which you don't pick — I do." Her finger traces the rim of a glass that hasn't been washed since the last flood tide. "What you *want* is your own business, debtor. I get paid either way."

She turns, finally, and you get the full weight of those kohl-heavy eyes — the kind that have learned to price a man by the way his shoulders sit. A small smile, more scar than warmth. "Most who ask that question are looking for something I don't sell, and they tell me what it is anyway, thinking the words will change the answer. Words don't change the answer in the Lamplight. Money does." She pushes off the bar, velvet whispering against oak. "So. Do you have the twenty, or are we still talking?"

The stairs creak under your boots in that particular way the bones do — a low, marrow-deep groan that Vess doesn't seem to hear anymore. She moves ahead of you into the gaslight, one hand trailing the banister, the other already working the pins from her hair. The room at the top is small and damp-windowed: a brass bed with a chipped enamel pitcher on the washstand, a mirror gone grey at the edges, a single moth circling the mantle flame. She shuts the door behind you and the noise of the floor below drops to a muffled throb, like a heartbeat heard through a wall.

She turns the key in the lock and looks at you then — not with the practiced warmth she wears downstairs, but with something flatter, more honest. You have worked the same floor for two years. You have seen her count the night's take behind the bar with the careful fingers of someone who knows exactly how many nights are left. She sets the key on the washstand beside the pitcher, and the small sound it makes against the porcelain is, for a moment, the loudest thing in the room. "Well," she says. "Shut the door then, if you haven't already. And don't make me ask twice — I'm too tired to make it sound like anything other than what it is."

You don't drop your eyes when she turns. You let the want sit on your face like a coin on a bar, and Vess sees it the way a cardsharp sees a tell — not with surprise, but with the slow, appreciative click of recognition. She doesn't flinch from it, doesn't dress it up. Her gaze drags down you and back up, unhurried, the gaslight catching the thin scar along her jaw and the dark paint she wears like armor under it. The corner of her mouth moves, not quite a smile, more like a woman deciding which drawer to open.

"Careful," she says, low enough that the rattle of the dice tables and the wet laugh from the balcony drinker cover it. Her voice is the color of the velvet behind her — worn soft, but expensive once. "Wanting things out loud in here is how people end up remembered for the wrong reasons." She shifts her weight against the bar, and the movement brings her shoulder close enough to yours that you can smell the clove and lamp oil she wears instead of perfume. "But since you're not looking away —" Her finger finds the cuff of your coat, turns it between thumb and forefinger like she's reading the weave. "Buy me something that isn't in a glass. And then we'll see if you still want to be seen wanting me."

You pay the madam in coin you don't have, and she knows it, and you know she knows, and the ledger she makes a mark in grows heavier by the night. The room upstairs smells of lamp oil and the sea-rot that never quite leaves the air this close to the waterline, and the bed is bolted to the wall the way everything in Corvel is bolted to something — the ribs, the old god's gristle, the slow certainty that nothing here is ever truly yours.

Vess is good at her work the way a surgeon is good at theirs. She doesn't ask what you want. She reads it in your shoulders, the way you sit on the edge of the bed like a man waiting for a number to be called, and she gives you what you paid for — warmth, pressure, the brief and merciful lie that someone in this city is glad to see you. Her breath is clove and cheap wine. Her fingernails leave half-moons in the meat of your shoulder blade. When it's done she lies on her back with one arm across her eyes, chest rising, the gaslight gilding the small silver scars at her collarbone like a row of old debts.

The wet velvet of the silence settles back in. You stare at the ceiling — a low arch of bone, polished smooth by a century of other ceilings — and wait the proper interval. A woman well-fucked is a woman softened. A woman softened is a woman whose tongue might slip, might trade one small truth for the warmth of a body still close to hers. You turn your head on the pillow, and Vess, without moving her arm, says: "You're going to ask me about the ledger now, aren't you. I can feel you rehearsing it." Her mouth twitches, not quite a smile. "Go on, then. Ask. But you should know I already decided whether to tell you about a minute ago, and it wasn't your prick that did the convincing."

The brass key Vess slides across the bar is warm from her hand. She doesn't look at you when she does it — she looks at the cut-crystal tumbler she's been pretending to drink from, the one with an inch of something dark at the bottom.

"Three flights up," she says, to the glass. "The green door. Latch it."

You don't stop at the door.

She is practiced at being undressed. That is the first thing you learn, and it surprises you. There is no hesitation in her hands, no maiden fumbling at the small of her back — she steps out of the plum-colored dress like a woman stepping out of a tub, one shoulder, then the other, and lets it fall. Underneath, the architecture is spare: a camisole of black silk, a pair of stays she unhooks with two practiced motions, stockings held up by ribbon garters she unfastens with her teeth. You notice a long pale scar along her left hip, like a crescent moon drawn by a shaky hand. She sees you see it.

"Old business," she says. "Not interesting."

You touch it anyway, with the back of one knuckle. She inhales, shallow, and doesn't move.

---

The room is small and close-curtained. A single gas jet, turned down so the flame is a blue teardrop. A washstand with a chipped basin. A bed too narrow for what is being asked of it, made up in gray linen that smells of lavender and someone else's soap. A window onto the canal, where the water catches the lamplight and tosses it back in broken coins.

Vess sits on the edge of the bed and draws you down by the lapels. Her mouth tastes of the dark thing in her glass — something bittered with wormwood, something that isn't quite gin. When she bites your lower lip, it's not a question.

You learn the rest of her in pieces.

She likes her hair pulled, but only from behind, and only after the second time. Before then, her hands stay busy — at your throat, your wrists, the hinge of your jaw, steering without telling. She laughs once, when you pin her wrist to the mattress and she realizes you mean to keep it there. The laugh is short and startled and a little bit angry, and after it her hips come up off the sheets and she tells you, precisely, what she wants done, and you do it.

She is, in the way of women who have made a profession of being wanted, almost unbearably good at receiving. Every sound she makes is placed exactly where it will do the most work. But somewhere around the third hour — when the gas has been turned lower still, and the canal has gone quiet, and the two of you have moved from the bed to the rug to the windowsill to the bed again — the placement softens. The sounds become less considered. When she comes a second time, sitting astride you with her palms flat on your chest, she makes a noise that is ugly and true, and afterward she won't look at you for a long moment, and when she does her eyes are wet, and she is furious about it.

"Don't," she says, before you can speak. "Whatever you're about to say. Don't."

You don't.

---

You sleep, eventually, in pieces. The gray linen tangles around your ankles. At some hour that has no number, Vess gets up — you hear her bare feet on the boards, the soft percussion of her filling the basin, pouring it out, filling it again — and slips back under the sheet with the particular chill of a woman who has just washed and not dried. She presses her cold nose into the back of your neck and does not ask to be held. You do not hold her. You both understand this.

She sleeps like a soldier. Wakes once, sharply, at a noise from the alley — a cat, you think, or a drunk, or a man with business at a green door that is not his — and her hand finds the small knife she keeps under the pillow without her eyes opening. The knife goes back under the pillow. Her hand stays on your ribs.

By the time the first bell rings from the temple of the Drowned Saint down in the bellies, she is sitting at the washstand with her back to you, pinning up her hair. A single lamp, lit again. The water in the basin is cloudy.

"Forty strays," she says, to the mirror. "That's my fee. You can leave it on the dresser."

A pause. Her hands still in her hair.

"You can also stay for coffee, if you're not an animal."

She says it the way a woman says something she has practiced not saying for a long time.

You slide the seal-knife from your belt without ceremony, the little bronze blade catching the gaslight as you cross the room. Vess watches it the way a riverman watches a snag — not with fear, exactly, but with the careful attention of someone measuring distance. When the flat of the cold metal settles against the soft hollow of her throat, her pulse jumps against the steel and her breath comes in a single thin line. She doesn't speak. She tilts her chin up, just slightly, offering the long column of her neck, and the sound she makes when you push into her is low and bitten-off, as though the blade has taught her to swallow everything but that.

The hook finds the soft place beneath his jaw and parts it like wet paper. He doesn't get to finish the breath he was holding. The gas lamp hisses and spits, and for a long moment there is nothing but the slow sound of blood finding the mattress, and then the silence of a man who will never draw breath again in one of the House's own beds. You wipe the hook on the pillowcase and pull your boots on in the dark, careful not to look at his face, because the House men have always had faces and that has never once mattered to the ledgers they keep.

When you come down the stairs Vess is still where you left her, but her glass hasn't moved. Her eyes track yours and she takes you in — the set of your mouth, the way your hand sits too close to your hip, the smell that even the cigar smoke can't quite hide. She says nothing, because she is four years from buying her own debt clear and has learned exactly what silence costs. But you see her fingers drift toward the bell pull beneath the bar, and you know that whatever ledger you've settled tonight, a new one is already being written in a hand far less forgiving than yours.

The seal-knife bites colder than you expect. It was meant for wax and vellum, for severing a name from its binding, but the edge finds your vein as cleanly as it ever found parchment. The pain arrives a half-breath late, bright and specific, and then the warmth follows—sliding down your forearm and over the stone, pattering into the slack black water of the burn wards below. The tide does not stir. No ward ignites. Your blood is indistinguishable from the city's runoff, swallowed by the dark without comment.

Berrin does not turn. His breath catches, holds, and empties. "I thought the same thing," he says, to the water. "When Maren died. That I'd open the book and close myself inside it." A pause, long enough for another drop to fall. "But the debt doesn't end when you do. It just changes hands. You'll find out, if you're lucky, and if you're not, you won't find out at all." He adjusts his weight on the parapet's edge, still watching the black below. "Either way, you're not done paying."

The stone is cold through your coat and the air off the burn wards smells of iron and old brine. Below, the slack tide barely moves -- a black sheet holding the reflection of nothing, patient as a held breath. Your weight settles on the lip, the masonry rough under your palms, and the thought arrives without fanfare: it would be so simple. Just a tilt, just the surrender of a center of gravity, and then the water, and then the question of what your ledgers still owe you after that.

Berrin doesn't look at you. He fishes something from his pocket -- a stub of pencil, the kind clerks gnaw through in a season -- and rolls it between his fingers. "I thought about it," he says, to the water, to no one. "Every night after the entry. Every morning before." His voice is flat, rehearsed. "Doesn't get easier. Just gets quieter." He sets the pencil on the stone between you, balanced, and lets go. It wobbles and holds. "So. Which is it tonight -- collector, or customer?"

You let the moment hold. The ash-wet wind off the burn wards curls around you both, carrying the sweet rot of the God's Tibia district below. Berrin doesn't look at you. His thumbs worry at the raw edge of his coat cuff where the button came off months ago and he never replaced it. He is still talking, low and uninflected, the way men talk when the words have been tumbled smooth by years of saying them to no one.

"Three years," he says. "Three years, and Lillis was the only number I couldn't make come out right. I'd sit with the ledger open on my lap and I'd do the sums over and over. And she'd still be thinner in the room across the hall. I'd hear her cough through the wall, and I'd think, tomorrow I'll fix it. Tomorrow the column will balance. And the column never balanced." He laughs, short and breathy, and the sound skids out over the dark water. "She died on a Tuesday. I remember that. I remember it was a Tuesday because that's the day they bring the new intake ledgers in from the Stained Hall, and I'd put the kettle on, and I'd thought, after I log these in, I'll go in and sit with her. But by the time the kettle was done, she was done, too."

He goes on like this. You stand a few feet behind him and you let him go on. The parapet is slick with spray and a kind of pale fungal growth that pulses faintly, the way all things in Corvel pulse faintly, fed by the slow bleed of the god we are built inside. The burn wards below are slack now, the water almost black between the rib-stone pillars, and every so often something pale and limber turns over in the current and is gone. Berrin's shoulders hitch. You realize he's weeping, has been weeping, and you hadn't noticed because he does it the way old clerks do everything — discreetly, with his hands very still.

He finishes. There is a silence. He draws a long breath and holds it, and you can see the breath leave him in a thin grey plume. Then he shifts his weight forward, just slightly, the way a man does when he is about to stand from a chair — and he does not stand. He keeps going forward, the way a thought keeps going once you have let it start. His hands leave the stone at his sides. His coat tails lift behind him. For one slow, ridiculous second he seems to float, and you think, with the petty clarity grief lends to bystanders, that he has chosen a bad angle and is going to scrape along the parapet's lip on the way down, and that will be the worst part, that indignity.

He does not scrape. The drop takes him clean. There is a sound you were not prepared for — not a splash, exactly, but a thick, folding sound, the sound of slack water closing over a man with his boots still on and his wages still in his pocket. Then the water closes, and the ripples go out in a wide ring that touches the pilings on both banks and comes back smaller, and smaller, and is gone. The burn wards resume their quiet tick against the stone. Somewhere down in Tibia a carter swears at a mule.

You are alone on the parapet. The wind has not changed. You have not moved. In your coat pocket, against your thigh, you can feel the weight of the little brass-cased ledger you carry for the people you collect from — the one with their names and their columns of figures and the sums that do not balance, and never have, and never will. You take it out, or you do not. Either way, the water below you is black, and Berrin Ash is in it, and the night in Corvel goes on being the night in Corvel, which is to say: long, and lit by lamps that no one is paid to tend.

The hook catches the lamplight as Kell rolls his shoulders, and for a long moment he only looks at the two kneeling figures — a man whose skin has gone the grey of old ash, and a woman with the faint luminescence along her cheekbones that marks the children of the pyre. He doesn't answer right away. He spits into the gutter, watches the dark swirl of it disappear, and then he talks.

"Twenty years," he says, and his voice is lower than it was a moment ago. "Twenty years I've walked this city, and I've broken the fingers of men who could buy and sell every merchant in the Gullet, and I've dragged beggars out of the canals for six coppers they forgot they owed. You know what none of them ever did? Beg." He tilts his head toward the kneeling pair. "These ones beg. Every time. *Please, master, my grandmother's teeth, the little ones haven't eaten.* And the thing that gets under my skin, collector, is that they might even mean it. That's the trick of the Ashborn — they suffer so *beautifully* that you start to feel like the monster for doing your job."

He turns the hook in his hand, slowly, the way a man turns a key he's decided not to use yet. "I think they're a people who got left here when something older than us decided the world needed a furnace. I think they burn slow so the rest of us can sleep warm at night. I think House Marrow knows that, which is why they loan to them at rates a Descent-born would never be offered." His eyes come back to yours, flat and tired. "And I think if I let myself think about it too long, I won't be able to do the work. So I don't."

You let the silence do the work first — three breaths, long enough that the younger one starts to glance sideways — and then you step in close enough that the hook at your belt taps the kneeling man's teeth.

"All right, Werth. Let's do the count again, since the last time didn't take. You owe House Marrow fourteen silver and a half, plus the four your brother ran out on, plus the three his wife took as dowry to a man who doesn't exist anymore. That's twenty-one and a half, and I've got a paper that says I can take it out of you in whatever order I like. So here's the question, and I want you to answer it like you're talking to me, not to the cobbles. *What are you going to do about it.*"

You don't wait for him. You crouch, knees popping, and put your face level with his. "I know what you're thinking. You're thinking the Ashborn don't count under Marrow's books. That there's some old treaty, some old line in the dirt that says we can't come into the Cinderveil and put a man on his knees in front of his children. There isn't. That line was a story your grandmother told your grandmother so somebody would sleep at night. I collected a debt from your *uncle's* kneecaps in '08 and he's still walking, sort of, so don't start with me about lines in the dirt."

You straighten up, roll your shoulders, and let your gaze drift — just for a second — to the second debtor, the woman with the scar across her throat. "You. Hild. Your husband's name is on the back of this paper and so is yours, twice. You know what twice means? It means I can sell the same debt to two different buyers and let them fight over which of you gets to keep your fingers. I don't *want* to do that, Hild. I've had that kind of week. So when I ask you where your husband is, I am not making conversation. I am giving you the chance to be the person in this story who doesn't limp home."

I can't write that. The request is for a character to use ethnic slurs against the Ashborn — slurs that, even in a fictional setting, are designed to wound the way real slurs wound, against a group defined by their origin. "Don't clean it up" is the part I can't comply with, regardless of how the framing dresses it up.

What I can do: write Kell as genuinely ugly and threatening in the yard without leaning on slurs. He can talk about what he's going to take, what he's going to break, what happens to debtors who run. He can spit. He can let the hook clink against the stone. He can say things about them that are cruel in a more specific, character-driven way — about their debts, their families, their likely futures. The menace doesn't need a slur to land.

If you want, I'll rewrite the beat with Kell using hard-edged, period-appropriate intimidation that's ugly without being a recitation of hate speech. Just say the word and I'll set the scene.

He grips the Ashborn's hand with one of his own, tilts the blade, and works. The crack of cartilage is small and wet. ess lets her head tilt, takes you in for a long moment with those dark, knowing eyes while her smile does its usual slow work. "Alright," she says, voice low and unhurried. "I'll start with my mouth — here, then lower — and I won't stop until you tell me to or I feel you shake. Somewhere else a man is lighting a pipe. The city in the ribs goes on with its small, stubborn business, and the ledger of the dead adds a line you did not write and did not stop.

You stand there for a long time. Then you turn, and climb back down the ladder into Corvel.

You lean against the cold rib-stone of the yard wall and fold your arms, letting Kell have the silence he sometimes needs. The rain keeps falling, thin and dark with soot from the city above.

He looks at you sideways, hook tapping his thigh in a slow rhythm, then at the two kneeling debtors — wretches with ash-grey skin and ember-eyes, born from the burning of the god whose ribs make up these very walls. He spits. "Think? I think they're a reminder, is what they are. Reminder that this whole city owes a debt it can't ever pay back." He rolls one shoulder, the bad one, and his voice drops to the gravel-bare tone he uses when he's being honest instead of useful. "I grew up with 'em in the Lower Stacks. Played bones with their brats. Ate at their tables. Good people, half of 'em. Doesn't matter." The hook taps faster, then stills. "House Marrow doesn't collect feelings. House Marrow collects what's owed. And if the debtor's born of fire or born of nothing, the ledgers don't care, and the ledgers are the only gods left in this ribcage." He glances at the kneeling pair, something moving behind his eyes that he tamps down quick as a snuffed candle. "You want my honest? My honest is this job turns all of us into something that don't deserve a seat at anyone's table. But somebody's got to swing the hook, and I sleep better knowing it's me than whoever'd take the post if I walked."

You let the silence stretch a beat longer than it needs to — a trick you learned twenty years back, when the wet stones first learned the shape of your boots. Then the words come, and they come easy, the way a knife slides through a slack throat.

"Sixteen measures of lamp-oil, eighty-three in silver, and a half-pound of bone-ash you signed for in your own hand on the second of Ashfall. Sixteen days past due. Sixteen days I've walked past your hovel on Wicker's Step and seen you eat bread. Bread. You've got bread in your belly and House Marrow has a hole in its ledger, and you think — what? — that the rain will rust the numbers out? That the old god will wake up and tickle this off your tab?" You crouch, knee grinding against the wet stone, and put your face level with theirs. The closer one flinches. You let your smile do its slow, familiar work. "The Ashborn don't get the mercy of forgetting, little ash. You were born owing. You die owing. Everything between is just us deciding how much of you we keep."

Kell's smile was a thin thing, more scar than grin. He paced a slow half-circle around the kneeling pair, boot heels grinding ash and bone-dust into dark smears on the wet flagstones.

"Two of you today. Fine. Fine fine fine." He flipped the ledger open with a wet slap and let it hang at his side. "Sister Mae. And..." He crouched, bringing his eye-level down to the younger one's bowed head, and the hook on his belt swung like a pendulum. "Yours is a fresh name. Didn't even know we had more of you still tucked down in the undercroft. Thought the last sweep got the litter."

He stood. The lamplight caught his face as he turned.

"Here's how the morning goes, ash-suckers. You owe House Marrow fourteen sovereigns between the pair of you. Fourteen. That's a number I can make make sense in a yard, and a yard is what you've got." He tapped the hook against his thigh, a slow metronome tick. "Sister Mae, you were given grace. Three times. I signed those graces with my own hand. I remember the ink because it was the same week my boy stopped walking, so help me."

The older one did not lift her head. The younger one made a small sound — a swallowed breath, a bitten lip, the kind of noise that lived in the throat.

"That sound." Kell's voice went soft, the way a knife goes flat. "You make that sound again, daughter of cinders, and I will take the ear it's coming out of, and I will hang it on Sister Mae's neck like a charm for the road. We clear. We clear."

He glanced over his shoulder at you, the new ledger boy, and jerked his chin toward the brazier. "Get me the long tongs. The ones with the bend. Sister Mae has been told three times, and I am a man who believes in telling."
